key_insight: Gliding-mammal-inspired wing and tail shapes create different aerodynamic trade-offs, with broader patagia maximizing lift and integrated or flat tails shifting control authority in different ways.
engineering_relevance: The study provides morphology-to-performance guidance for bioinspired morphing aerial vehicles, helping designers balance lift, drag, stall behavior, and maneuverability.
method: Used computational fluid dynamics to isolate aerodynamic effects of representative gliding-mammal morphologies.
Compared three patagium outlines for lift, drag, stall, and pitching moment.
Tested three tail/uropatagium designs under baseline, symmetric-deflection, and asymmetric-deflection conditions for longitudinal and lateral control.
evidence_signal: The abstract reports comparative CFD evaluation showing the broadest patagium produced the highest lift, while the intermediate shape had smoother post-stall behavior and the tail designs differed in pitch, roll, and yaw authority depending on deflection mode.
watch_item: Because the results come from controlled CFD comparisons, real-world performance may change with unmodeled flexibility, turbulence, Reynolds-number effects, and flight dynamics.
paper_title: Patagium and tail morphology shape aerodynamic performance and control authority in gliding-mammal-inspired wings
